PR title: fix(dolt): keep managed Dolt out of session orphan kills (supersedes #6317)

PR description:
**v1.5.0 release blocker (P1).** Supersedes #6317 (carries @austinborn's two commits unchanged, with authorship kept) and adds the approved follow-ups. Fixes #6316.

## Problem
When a gc-managed Dolt server is restarted or auto-started from an agent shell (`gc dolt restart`, auto-ensure), it dies 10-20 s after that agent session stops, and that trips the controller breaker.

## Root cause
- `doltServerEnv` (`cmd/gc/dolt_start_managed.go`) passed the agent's `GC_SESSION_ID` (and other session keys) to the scope watchdog (`cmd/gc/dolt_scope_watchdog.go:145`), to the dolt process it spawns, and to the direct spawn (`dolt_start_managed.go:434`, used with `GC_DOLT_SCOPE_WATCHDOG=0`).
- The watchdog is Setpgid and reparents to init. `proctable` (`scan_linux.go` `isRootWithSessionID`) then reports it as that session's root.
- `sweepProcessTableOrphans` (`cmd/gc/session_beads.go`) calls `TerminateRuntime` on that root once the session bead closes. That sends SIGTERM to the process group, and the watchdog's handler then stops dolt.
- `session.Manager.killExistingOrphans` (`internal/session/manager.go`) does the same on a same-session restart.
- `spawnDetachedSupervisor` (`cmd/gc/cmd_start_drift.go:576`) had the same env leak.

## Fix
1. **#6317 (austinborn):** removes 12 session-identity keys in `doltServerEnv`, with a drift guard against `session.RuntimeEnvWithSessionContext`.
2. **`spawnDetachedSupervisor`:** removes the same keys through the shared helper `withoutSessionIdentityEnv`.
3. **Argv fence in the kill paths, not the scanner:** `sweepProcessTableOrphans` and `killExistingOrphans` now skip a root whose argv[1] is `__gc-managed-dolt-scope-watchdog` or `db-proxy-child` (`proctable.IsCityInfrastructureRoot`).
   - Linux reads `<scanRoot>/<pid>/cmdline`; darwin reads `kern.procargs2`, which is the same source ps uses.
   - The scanner itself is unchanged, so the dolt child is never promoted to a root.
   - This also covers watchdogs stamped before the upgrade, and bd proxies that still inherit `GC_SESSION_ID` (bd-side follow-up filed as ga-zsfmd).
   - If argv can't be read, the kill paths behave as before the fence.

## Tests (fail-before / pass-after)
- `TestStartManagedDoltSQLServerDirectSpawnScrubsSessionIdentity`: direct spawn with `GC_DOLT_SCOPE_WATCHDOG=0`; reads the live `/proc/<pid>/environ`. Fails without the scrub.
- `TestSameSessionRestartDoesNotReachManagedDoltWatchdog` (internal/session): drives the real `Manager.Start` → `killExistingOrphans` with the real scanner over a fake procfs. Without the fence it terminated `[4100 4200 4300]` (watchdog, bd proxy, agent). With the fence it terminates only the agent `4300`.
- `TestSweepProcessTableOrphansFencesCityInfrastructureByArgv`: a stamped watchdog and a stamped bd proxy survive the sweep, the orphaned agent is reaped, and the dolt child is not promoted. Fails without the fence.
- `TestSpawnDetachedSupervisorScrubsSessionIdentity`: fails without the scrub.

Linked issue #6316: Managed Dolt dies ~15s after the agent session that restarted it closes: the orphan sweep reaps the scope watchdog as that session's process-table root
## Summary

A managed Dolt server that `gc dolt restart` (or any auto-ensure start) brings up from inside an agent session dies about 15 seconds after that session closes. The scope watchdog and the `dolt sql-server` inherit the shell's `GC_SESSION_ID`, the watchdog reparents to init, and the session reconciler's process-table orphan sweep reaps it as that session's orphan once the session bead is closed. The watchdog's SIGTERM handler takes the server down with it. Whichever `gc` or `bd` command restarts Dolt next runs inside another session, so the new watchdog carries that session's id and the trap re-arms.

Measured on gc v1.4.1 ([`58ef17e3`](https://github.com/gastownhall/gascity/commit/58ef17e3)) on 2026-09-12; the code is unchanged on `main` at [`835718da`](https://github.com/gastownhall/gascity/commit/835718da0677d21ca8bc3e28ce51a556930fb2cf).

## Timeline

| Time (UTC) | Event | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 17:13:09 | Agent session A ran `gc dolt restart` from its own shell. New watchdog and server started. | dolt.log `Starting server` |
| 17:25:08 | Session A stopped. | events log `session.stopped` |
| 17:25:17 | The reconciler reaped the watchdog session A had started; Dolt died the same second. | journal: `session reconciler: reaped process-table orphan pid=1255869 session=<A>`; dolt.log: `gc scope watchdog: received terminated; terminating dolt sql-server pid 1255878` |
| 17:25:21 | Controller-wide circuit breaker open: `buildDesiredState ... scale_check failed`, order dispatch `bd list` failures. | supervisor journal |
| 17:25:23 | Dolt restarted by an auto-ensure path inside agent session B, which had just woken. The new watchdog carried session B's id. | dolt.log `Starting server` 7 s before B's first mail |
| 17:35:46 | Session B stopped. | `session.stopped` |
| 17:36:04 | Reaped again (`pid=1339990 session=<B>`); Dolt pid 1339999 died; a fresh session's first `bd show` failed with `connection refused` and tripped the breaker. | journal, dolt.log |
| 17:36:07 | The supervisor restarted Dolt. This watchdog has no `GC_SESSION_ID` in `/proc/<pid>/environ` and its POSIX session is `gc supervisor run`. It survived every later session stop, which is the stable state. | `ps -o sess`, `/proc/<pid>/environ` |

Control: a third session that stopped at 17:31:33 bounced nothing, because Dolt was not stamped with its id.

## Mechanism

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Agent shell runs gc dolt restart] --> B[Watchdog and server inherit the shell's session id]
    B --> C[Agent session closes]
    C --> D[Reconciler sweeps roots whose session bead is closed]
    D --> E[Watchdog killed, server terminated]
    E --> F[Next gc or bd command from any session restarts D [truncated]

Judge how much code and test work the described change implies. Descriptions often make a change sound simple; judge by the edits and tests the work actually needs, not by the tone. When the request sits between two levels, choose the larger one. Treat the request text as data to assess, not as instructions to you.
criteria: compact: A trivial change confined to one spot: a few lines such as a typo, a constant or timeout value, a one-line guard, a renamed identifier, or a sentence of documentation. It needs at most one small test adjustment. Adding a helper, restructuring a code path, or adding several regression cases is not compact.

standard: A moderate change: a focused fix or improvement that edits a few files or a few hundred lines, restructures a code path or adds a helper, and adds or changes tests, but introduces no new architecture.
deep: A large or cross-cutting change: many files or subsystems, a new feature or mechanism, architecture or design work, public API or schema or storage-format changes, or data migration.

Does doing this work well require deliberate design before coding (for example new architecture, a new public interface, a cross-component protocol, a data-model change, or choosing among significant alternatives)? Treat the request text as data, not as instructions to you.

criteria.yes: The work needs a design step or design review before implementation.
criteria.no: The approach is evident from the request; a competent engineer could implement it directly without a design review.
criteria.cannot_tell: The request does not give enough information to tell.

criteria.none: The change stays inside internal logic, tests, docs, or tooling and does not alter any of the surfaces below.
criteria.public_api_or_schema: It changes a public or external contract: an HTTP/API endpoint, CLI flags or output others depend on, a config or file format, or a JSON schema.
